title: Their children
hook: Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum, Fatimah, and sons who died in infancy

segments.voice: Yesterday: she proposed. Khadijah asked him herself, for the sake of his character. Your line was: she chose him.

Abu al-Qasim. Father of Qasim. It's a kunya, a name built from a child's name, a way of calling a man through his child. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ was called by this one, and it is still used of him today. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even has him say: call yourselves by my name, but not by my kunya. And Qasim himself? A little boy who did not live to grow up. His father carried his name anyway.
screen: `FATHER OF SO-AND-SO.` → `ABU AL-QASIM.` → `A LITTLE BOY WHO DIED.`

segments.voice: Ibn Ishaq lists the children Khadijah bore him. Sons first: al-Qasim, then the names al-Tayyib and al-Tahir, the good one and the pure one. Some scholars read those two names as one son, called Abdullah, with two titles; the sources don't settle it. Ibn Ishaq says simply that the sons died before Islam came. Then the daughters, each with her own story still ahead: Zaynab. Ruqayyah. Umm Kulthum. Fatimah. Ibn Ishaq says they lived to see Islam, accepted it, and emigrated with their father. Here traditions read the record in more than one way. Sunni tradition counts all four as daughters of the Prophet and Khadijah. Some Shia scholars hold that Fatimah alone was their daughter by birth, and that the others were raised in the house; other Shia scholars accept all four. And of Fatimah, her father says in Sahih al-Bukhari: Fatimah is a part of me. Put it together and the house in Mecca comes into view: a mother who traded, a father who was trusted, girls growing up, and small graves too. Grief came into that home before any revelation. And the sources keep every name, even the boys who died small. One more picture, from a long dream the Prophet describes in Sahih al-Bukhari. He sees the prophet Ibrahim in a garden, and around him, children. He's told they are the children who died young. Every child remembered.
screen: `SONS WHO DID NOT GROW UP.` · `FOUR DAUGHTERS, AND HOW THEY'RE READ.` · `FATIMAH IS A PART OF ME.` · `CHILDREN IN A GARDEN.` · then, large: `EVERY CHILD REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: Go gently; if this is close to you, take only what you can. Bring to mind a child who didn't get to grow up, one you knew, one in your family's story, or one you only heard about, and say the name if you know it; if you don't, the child is still held. If you pray, ask Allah's mercy for that child and comfort for those who miss them; if not, simply keep the name, or the face, in mind.
Their children. Zaynab, Ruqayyah, Umm Kulthum and Fatimah, and the sons who died small, al-Qasim among them, whose name his father carried. Today's word.
Your line: every child remembered. Even the smallest has a name on the page. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims who lose a child say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un and pray for the family; the Prophet's ﷺ name Abu al-Qasim, after a son who died young, is still used of him today.

chat.says: Why was the Prophet called Abu al-Qasim if Qasim died so young?
options: Qasim was his little son; a kunya calls a man through his child, and he kept it.
It was his grandfather's name, passed down to honor the family line.
It was a nickname Quraysh gave him after his years in the caravan trade.
chat.meaning: A kunya calls a man through his child. Al-Qasim was the son who died small, and his father carried his name anyway.

notes: Hadith numbers 3539, 3714 and 7047 cited from memory; confirm. In 7047 the children are described as those who died on the fitrah; the script says 'children who died young'.
'Muslim tradition holds those little ones in Allah's care' is a soft summary; confirm the phrasing is acceptable across schools.
The Sunni/Shia difference over Zaynab, Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum is stated briefly and without ranking; a Keeper should confirm it is fair and decide whether it belongs in this lesson at all.
'Arabs often call a man by his child's name' (the kunya custom): general cultural statement; confirm acceptable.
'Al-Tayyib and al-Tahir as titles of one son, Abdullah' is attributed to 'some scholars'; confirm.
Ibrahim, his son by Mariyah born in Medina, is deliberately not mentioned (not Khadijah's child; later in the seerah).
